newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Seats come with shares in Sydney Olympic offer.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Seats come with shares in Sydney Olympic offer.

text.p: The consortium building Sydney's Olympic stadium launched a public share offer with a difference on Tuesday -- subscribers will be guaranteed seats at the showpiece events of the 2000 Games.

In a pioneering Olympic financing scheme, the Australia Stadium group said it was hoping to raise A$364.4 million by selling packages that have Olympic seats, long-term stadium club membership and share equity attached.

A total 34,400 gold passes will be sold for A$10,000 each, giving initial subscribers a seat at every stadium session of the Games, including the opening and closing ceremonies and the men's 100-metres sprint final.
Buyers will enjoy stadium club membership for 30 years after the Games, allowing them to attend dozens of sports events every year at no extra cost except for an annual fee of around A$300.
They will also get 1,000 shares in the stadium company itself, which will be publicly listed on the Australian stock exchange.
Better-off sports fans with a spare A$33,000 will be able to buy one of 600 platinum passes with two top-class seats attached and even more membership privileges over the following 30 years.

"What Sydney is getting here through this innovative financial arrangement is an Olympic stadium that will cost the taxpayers nothing, or very little," stadium company chairman Peter Ritchie told a news conference to launch the share offer four years ahead of the Games.

With the regional government underwriting the Games and large television and marketing revenunes already in the bag, Sydney organisers appear to have avoided the money problems that hit this year's Atlanta Olympics.

The share offer cuts government investment in the A$615 million stadium construction to just under $100 million. Gold pass investors will contribute A$283.8 million after deduction of underwriting costs and will hold 35.4 percent of Australia Stadium Management capital. Platinum members will hold 1.2 percent.

The founding members of the stadium consortium -- Multiplex Constructions Pty Ltd, Hambros Australia Limited, Macquarie Corporate Finance Ltd and Japan's Obayashi Corporation -- will hold 29.4 percent, of the capital.
The remaining 34 percent will be held by three commercial investors, facilities manager Ogden IFC, caterers Gardner Merchant and soft drinks giant Coca-Cola Amatil.

Gold pass customers will be able to sell their shares when the company is listed on the Australian Stock Exchange, probably next year but they would then lose their club membership rights. They will retain their Olympic tickets, which cannot be sold.
From 1999, when the stadium opens for business, investors will be able to sell off their club memberships and shares separately. The company will run a market in memberships.

Company officials declined to break down the value of the various components of the package, but Ritchie said buying comparable tickets to every stadium session in Atlanta would have cost around A$6,000.

He said the company's board -- former rugby union star Mark Ella and 1968 Olympic 800 metres champion Ralph Doubell are both non-executive directors -- are keen that investors use their membership to the full after the Olympics are over.
"We don't want silvertails (rich people) sitting on memberships they never use," Ricthie said.

He denied a Sydney newspaper report that the 600 platinum packages had already been snapped up by the "big end of town", especially well-off clients of the stockbroking firms underwriting the share offer.
